A1-A2.headline: How Alexander Fleming Discovered Penicillin By Accident

pages.text: Penicillin is a famous medicine. Doctors use it to stop dangerous germs. It comes from a natural mould. Before this discovery, many people died from simple cuts and illnesses.
pages.caption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin.

imageProvenance.credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/12/d4/a9331961bf9ec04b09fa2f7fffb8.jpg archive Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0059573.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-29): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/xkbnmutd C

evidence.fileTitle: File:Glass phial of British Standard penicillin, London, England, Wellcome L0059573.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin

pages.text: In 1928, a Scottish doctor named Alexander Fleming worked in a London hospital. He left some small glass plates with germs on a table before going on holiday. When he came back, a green mould was growing on one plate. The germs near the mould were dead. The mould made a special juice that killed them.
pages.caption: Alexander Fleming in his London laboratory.

evidence.articleCaption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, in 1943
evidence.articleSection: Discovery of the properties of mould juice

pages.text: Fleming wrote about his finding, but he could not make enough medicine in his small lab. In 1939, a team of scientists at Oxford University read his work. Howard Florey led this team. They learned how to grow and clean the mould so it was safe for people.
pages.caption: Howard Florey during his research work.

imageProvenance.credit: Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Penicillin Past, Present and Future- the Development and Production of Penicillin, England, 1944 D17803.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Howard Florey in his office in 1944

pages.text: During the Second World War, factories started making large amounts of penicillin. This new medicine helped treat hurt soldiers. It saved thousands of lives. Soon, hospitals everywhere had the medicine.
pages.caption: Glass vessels used to grow penicillin mould.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Penicillin fermentation vessel, England Wellcome L0059171.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Thousands of glass fermentation vessels like this one were used in laboratories to produce penicillin. The mould was grown on the surface of a liquid filled with nutrients. The stopper kept contaminants out while allowing the mould to get fresh air.

pages.text: In 1945, Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey, and Ernst Chain won the Nobel Prize for their work. Penicillin changed modern medicine and helped create many other treatments used today.

B1-B2.headline: The Remarkable Story Behind the Discovery of Penicillin

pages.text: The history of penicillin represents one of the most significant breakthroughs in modern medicine. Long before laboratories existed, ancient cultures observed that certain moulds and plants could help heal infected wounds. However, early practitioners could never isolate the active substances responsible for these healing properties.
pages.caption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin.

imageProvenance.credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/12/d4/a9331961bf9ec04b09fa2f7fffb8.jpg archive Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0059573.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-29): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/xkbnmutd C

evidence.fileTitle: File:Glass phial of British Standard penicillin, London, England, Wellcome L0059573.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin

pages.text: A major turning point occurred in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital in London. Scottish physician Alexander Fleming was investigating bacterial cultures when he left for a summer holiday. During his absence, an airborne mould spore contaminated one of his culture dishes. Upon his return, Fleming noticed a clear halo surrounding the mould where bacteria had failed to survive.
pages.caption: Alexander Fleming in his London laboratory.

evidence.articleCaption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, in 1943
evidence.articleSection: Discovery of the properties of mould juice

pages.text: Although Fleming identified the antibacterial potential of the mould juice, he lacked the chemical resources to purify it. In 1939, a dedicated research team at Oxford University, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, revisited Fleming's early papers. They successfully cultivated the mould, extracted the active compound, and demonstrated its remarkable safety and effectiveness in animal trials.
pages.caption: Howard Florey during his research work.

imageProvenance.credit: Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Penicillin Past, Present and Future- the Development and Production of Penicillin, England, 1944 D17803.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Howard Florey in his office in 1944

pages.text: Transforming a laboratory curiosity into a practical medicine required immense industrial effort. During the Second World War, American and British researchers developed mass-production techniques using large fermentation vessels. This coordinated manufacturing effort ensured that adequate supplies reached Allied soldiers on the front lines, ultimately saving countless lives.
pages.caption: Glass vessels used to grow penicillin mould.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Penicillin fermentation vessel, England Wellcome L0059171.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Thousands of glass fermentation vessels like this one were used in laboratories to produce penicillin. The mould was grown on the surface of a liquid filled with nutrients. The stopper kept contaminants out while allowing the mould to get fresh air.

pages.text: In recognition of their monumental contributions, Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey, and Ernst Chain were jointly awarded the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The widespread availability of penicillin transformed healthcare globally, proving that cooperative scientific research could conquer previously incurable bacterial diseases.

C1-C2.headline: From Serendipitous Observation to Therapeutic Paradigm

pages.text: The historical trajectory of penicillin illustrates the intricate transition from empirical folk remedies to rigorous antimicrobial chemotherapy. While ancient societies across diverse civilizations empirically recognized the therapeutic efficacy of various moulds, they lacked the methodological framework required to isolate active biochemical principles.
pages.caption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin.

imageProvenance.credit: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/12/d4/a9331961bf9ec04b09fa2f7fffb8.jpg archive Gallery: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/image/L0059573.html Wellcome Collection gallery (2018-03-29): https://wellcomecollection.org/works/xkbnmutd C

evidence.fileTitle: File:Glass phial of British Standard penicillin, London, England, Wellcome L0059573.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Glass vial of British Standard penicillin

pages.text: The seminal breakthrough materialized in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital, London, where Alexander Fleming observed the inhibition of Staphylococcus aureus by a contaminating Penicillium spore. Although Fleming documented this antagonistic phenomenon and designated the active principle penicillin, limitations in biochemical techniques precluded successful isolation at that time.
pages.caption: Alexander Fleming in his London laboratory.

evidence.articleCaption: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, London, in 1943
evidence.articleSection: Discovery of the properties of mould juice

pages.text: A decisive multidisciplinary initiative was launched in 1939 at the Sir William Dunn School of Pathology, Oxford. Spearheaded by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, the research collective systematically refined cultivation methods, purification protocols, and biological assays, verifying that the extract disrupted bacterial cell division without compromising mammalian leukocytes.
pages.caption: Howard Florey during his research work.

imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer Ministry of Information Photo Division Photographer (Public domain)

evidence.articleCaption: Howard Florey in his office in 1944

pages.text: Scaling production from laboratory vessels to industrial fermentation during the Second World War required unprecedented international cooperation between academic institutions, agricultural laboratories, and private enterprise. This mobilization ensured a reliable therapeutic supply, significantly mitigating wartime mortality rates.
pages.caption: Glass vessels used to grow penicillin mould.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Penicillin fermentation vessel, England Wellcome L0059171.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Thousands of glass fermentation vessels like this one were used in laboratories to produce penicillin. The mould was grown on the surface of a liquid filled with nutrients. The stopper kept contaminants out while allowing the mould to get fresh air.

pages.text: Subsequent elucidation of the molecular architecture by Dorothy Hodgkin facilitated the synthesis of derivatives. However, the contemporaneous emergence of bacterial resistance observed by the Oxford team underscored an enduring pharmacological challenge that continues to drive contemporary antimicrobial research.
